subject: [DISCUSS] Human Summary section in agent-drafted PR descriptions

messages.subject: [DISCUSS] Human Summary section in agent-drafted PR descriptions
messages.body:
Hello everyone,

Following the objection in the [LAZY CONSENSUS] thread, I am turning
this into a discussion. The change (#73660) has already been reverted
in #73669 (thanks Ash) - and apologies for merging it before the lazy
consensus ended; I thought it was uncontroversial, which it clearly
is not.

The original proposal, for PR descriptions drafted by AI agents:

* The description starts with a short "Human Summary" - a few
  sentences typed by the human author, in their own words: why the
  change is needed, key decisions, caveats.
* The agent-written description stays below it, in an "AI Summary"
  section folded by default.
* Agents are instructed to ask the author for the Human Summary and
  paste it verbatim - never to write, suggest or paraphrase it.

Ash's objection, as I understand it: the PR description should already
be written for humans, and it is how the author engages with the
community - so an explicitly labelled "Human Summary" reverses the
priority. His counter-proposal is to drop both the "Human Summary"
and "AI Summary" headers and put the agent text in a folded
<details><summary>AI Summary</summary> block.

I see it the other way round. Following the ASF Generative Tooling
guidance, we already require every such PR to state that it was
generated with AI - the reader knows up front that an agent was
involved. Given that, an explicit "Human Summary" is exactly the
signal that matters: it shows that the human was driving the change,
and that they understand it well enough to summarize - in their own
words - what the PR does and why. Without the label, the reader of an
AI-disclosed PR has no way to tell which part the author actually
wrote. This is the "centaur" - human in control - not the "reverse
centaur" or "meat proxy" [1].

Looking at it again, the two proposals are closer than it seems: both
put the author's own words on top and fold the agent's text below.
The actual differences are:

1. Should the human-written part be explicitly labelled
   ("Human Summary") so it is distinguishable in an AI-disclosed PR,
   or just be the unlabelled top of the description?
2. Should the folded agent text be marked "AI Summary" (Ash suggests
   the <details> summary label - that part we seem to agree on)?
3. Should agents be required to ask for the human part and refuse to
   draft it themselves - or should that be left to the author?

Just to remind - this is **only** for PRs that are agenically generated.
If someone creates their PRs manually, without the AI agent, none of
this applies.

The template for PRs opened via GH UI is not supposed to have either section.

I'd love to hear what others think - especially those who review a lot
of agent-assisted PRs, and Shahar, who has been using this format
already.

[1] https://doctorow.medium.com/https-pluralistic-net-2025-09-11-vulgar-thatcherism-there-is-an-alternative-f1428b42a8fd

J.

messages.subject: Re: [DISCUSS] Human Summary section in agent-drafted PR descriptions
messages.body:
Ash - I understand your approach, and not against the formulation that you
suggested (without headers + changing "Click here" to "AI Summary").
However, I think that it will be easier for contributors to comprehend that
they should write the description in their own words if there's an explicit
instruction for doing that. If you're against headers, it could also be in
the form of an HTML comment like we already do in other areas (i.e., <!--
YOU MUST WRITE THIS SECTION WITHOUT LLM -->).
Personally, I think that headers will have a better effect as they are more
visible (for both author and reviewers altogether).



Shahar

messages.subject: Re: [DISCUSS] Human Summary section in agent-drafted PR descriptions
messages.body:
Hi all,

Just wanted to chime in with an idea related to the topic of human
summaries. The proposal above is mainly focused on PR descriptions but
I feel we should apply a similar concept to PR reviews and general
communication, encouraging users to write their own reviews and
responses. If you can't explain it in your own words, should you still
be involving yourself? Doesn't mean you can't use AI but at least some
human interaction. I think most people are also more receptive when
they see there is actual human interaction (as Jarek mentioned on
Slack), rather than receiving a response from an agent. I know there
is already a maintainer PR triage process in place which typically
involves an automated first pass so I'm not implying maintainers
should have to adhere to this (that would be counterproductive).

There are obviously counter arguments to this. If someone is willing
to spend their own tokens and it actually helps move things along then
is it actually a problem? Some people also express themselves better
in their native tongue and might use AI to help translate to english.
Those are just a few that came to my mind.

If this is something the community feels is important to encourage,
then I think a good first step could be to extend some of the language
in the contributing docs. In regards to reviews, the docs mainly just
encourage reviewing but don't mention anything about AI. Same can be
said for the how to communicate docs. Curious to hear everyone's
thoughts.

- Justin P

messages.subject: Re: [DISCUSS] Human Summary section in agent-drafted PR descriptions
messages.body:
Hi everyone,

I think we should seriously consider distinguishing between two types
of contributors:

1.  Transactional Contributors: People who simply want to fix a
specific issue they are facing.
2.  Community Contributors: People who genuinely want to be part of
the community, help make product decisions, engage with other members,
learn, and share knowledge.

For the first group, I see great potential in leveraging AI to process
and validate contributions with minimal human overhead. With thousands
of issues that users want to solve, AI tools now make it feasible to
generate reliable fixes. Everyone benefits as long as we establish
automated workflows to review, test, and accept these contributions
without consuming valuable maintainer time. The more we can automate
this layer, the stronger the project's foundation will be.

For the second group, we need a clear path that allows these
contributors to move past initial automated gates and connect directly
with maintainers. Once we offload the transactional review workload,
we can dedicate almost 100% of our human attention to meaningful,
human-to-human community interactions.

To achieve this, our discussions should shift away from line-by-line
code reviews. AI agents and automated harnesses are already better
suited for checking code invariants, conventions, and implementation
details. Instead, maintainers should focus on higher-level priorities:
assessing intention, discussing long-term vision, defining project
boundaries, and designing the automated guardrails.

I would love to hear your thoughts and discuss ideas on how we can
automate transactional fixes so we can focus our time on the broader
"why" behind our project.

I think the difficulty lies mainly in separating contributions of type
1 from 2. And maybe we should think how to make it more "obvious"
which is which.

Best regards,
Jarek

> > > >> The original proposal, for PR descriptions drafted by AI agents:
> > > >>
> > > >> * The description starts with a short "Human Summary" - a few
> > > >>  sentences typed by the human author, in their own words: why the
> > > >>  change is needed, key decisions, caveats.
> > > >> * The agent-written description stays below it, in an "AI Summary"
> > > >>  section folded by default.
> > > >> * Agents are instructed to ask the author for the Human Summary and
> > > >>  paste it verbatim - never to write, suggest or paraphrase it.
> > > >>
> > > >> Ash's objection, as I understand it: the PR description should already
> > > >> be written for humans, and it is how the author engages with the
> > > >> community - so an explicitly labelled "Human Summary" reverses the
> > > >> priority. His counter-proposal is to drop both the "Human Summary"
> > > >> and "AI Summary" headers and put the agent text in a folded
> > > >> <details><summary>AI Summary</summary> block.
> > > >>
> > > >> I see it the other way round. Following the ASF Generative Tooling
> > > >> guidance, we already require every such PR to state that it was
> > > >> generated with AI - the reader knows up front that an agent was
> > > >> involved. Given that, an explicit "Human Summary" is exactly the
> > > >> signal that matters: it shows that the human was driving the change,
> > > >> and that they understand it well enough to summarize - in their own
> > > >> words - what the PR does and why. Without the label, the reader of an
> > > >> AI-disclosed PR has no way to tell which part the author actually
> > > >> wrote. This is the "centaur" - human in control - not the "reverse
> > > >> centaur" or "meat proxy" [1].
> > > >>
> > > >> Looking at it again, the two proposals are closer than it seems: both
> > > >> put the author's own words on top and fold the agent's text below.

> > > >>
> > > >> 1. Should the human-written part be explicitly labelled
> > > >>   ("Human Summary") so it is distinguishable in an AI-disclosed PR,
> > > >>   or just be the unlabelled top of the description?
> > > >> 2. Should the folded agent text be marked "AI Summary" (Ash suggests
> > > >>   the <details> summary label - that part we seem to agree on)?
> > > >> 3. Should agents be required to ask for the human part and refuse to
> > > >>   draft it themselves - or should that be left to the author?
> > > >>
> > > >> Just to remind - this is **only** for PRs that are agenically generated.
> > > >> If someone creates their PRs manually, without the AI agent, none of
